metadata.response:
### Question 1

Which statement about quick sort is correct?
- A. It rearranges the array into two parts around a chosen pivot element.
- B. It is a stable sorting algorithm in every implementation.
- C. It runs in linear time on every input of size n.
- D. It requires the input array to be already sorted.

**Answer:** A

**Explanation:** Quick sort works by choosing a pivot and partitioning the array so that elements smaller than the pivot come before it and larger elements come after it; the two parts are then sorted recursively. This is why option A is correct. Quick sort is not stable in its standard in-place form (B is false), its average cost is O(n log n) with a worst case of O(n²), never linear in general (C is false), and it works on any input, sorted or not (D is false).

### Question 2

Fill in the blank: When sorting an array of $n$ elements, merge sort requires ____ comparisons in the worst case, regardless of the initial order of the input.

**Answer:** Θ(n log n)

**Explanation:** Merge sort always splits the array into two halves (about $\log_2 n$ levels of recursion) and each level performs a linear $\Theta(n)$ amount of merging work. Multiplying the levels by the work per level gives $\Theta(n \log n)$ comparisons in the worst case. Unlike quick sort, this bound does not depend on the input order, because the split is always made at the midpoint rather than around a pivot.
